3. The facts relevant to dispose of the rule in short are that the opposite party No. 1 filed a miscellaneous case no. 18 of 1986 which was subsequently renumbered as Misc. Case No. 33 of 1984 for pre-emption stating that he is a co-sharer of the case holding by purchase and did not know of the transfer and no notice Was served upon him. Subsequently he came to know about the transfer. Opposite party No. 2 sold the case land to Opposite party No. 1. Therefore he took certified copy of the deed on 24.12.1975 and then he filed this pre-emption case. Opposite party No. 1 i.e. the present petitioner contested the suit by filling written objection wherein he stated that the pre-emptee petitioner had knowledge of the transfer and that after purchase he has constructed a 15' x 50' sami pacca tin shed on the plot no. 3178 and conducting business there. He also stated that the suit was bad for defect of parties and as such the pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed. The learned Assistant judge after considering the evidences on record found the case was not maintainable for defect of parties and as such he disallowed the pre-emption case by his order dated 28.2.1987. Against this order opposite party. No. 1 preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal no. 22 of 1987 before the District judge and the same was heard by the learned subordinate judge who his order dated 3.3.1989 allowed the appeal and sent the case back on remand with a direction upon the learned Assistant judge to hear the case afresh alter giving opportunity to both sides and to remove the defect of parties. Being aggrieved at and dissatisfied with the order of the appellate court the petitioner preferred this application under section 115 of the code of Civil procedure and obtained the present rule. 

 5. The plain reading of this order shows at when an appeal is preferred against .a decree upon a preliminary point and that decree is reversed in an appeal, the appellate court may, if thinks fit, sent the case, back or remand to the trial court. In this instant case appeal was not preferred against any decision of preliminary point. The trial court decided all the points at issue after discussing the evidences on record and arrived at a finding that the case bad for defect of parties. Moreover it appears from the trial courts judgment that the present petitioner said that by exhibited documents Ext. A and B one Nazrul Jalil Biswas sold his share to one person of Bhimnagar. Moreover defect of parties has already been stated in paragraph-8 of his written objection. The opposite party No. 1 did not make those purchasers as necessary parties during trial of the case. The trial court knew about it. 

 6. The learned Advocate Md. Nurul Hoque for the opposite party submitted that there is no bar to add party in a pre-emption case at any stage of the case and the appellate court decided for sending the case back on remand only because pre-emption of a bonafide pre-emptor cannot be refused. In support of the above contention he referred to a case reported in 31 D.L.R. (AD)-88 (Akhtarun Nessa and another Vs. Habibullah and other) where-in their lordships held. It is the requirement of the statute that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties, but a case of pre-emption under section 96 may not be defeated on the analogy of non-joinder of all co-sharer in a suit for partition. The reason is obvious, because, in .a suit for partition non-joinder of a co-sharer may prove fatal to the suit. But position in a pre-emption case is different. Right of pre-emption accrues on a transfer of a portion or share of holding of a raiyat or when a holding is transferred which gives rise to an application for pre-emption either under the first part or second part of sub-section (10) of section 96. This right is not absolute but subject to the right of other co-sharers and holders of land contiguous to the land transferred, as the case may be, requirement of the statue of imp leading has in who favour right of pre-emption accrued is for the sole purpose of enabling the court to adjudicate the claim of all the par-ties having right to pre-empt according to the provision under section (5) of section 90 in one proceeding and avoiding multiplicity of proceedings., So, for the sake of full and complete adjudication of the rights and granting relief, there should not be absence of any necessary party. In this instant case the opposite party No. I knew about the defect of parties at the time of trial before the learned Assistant judge but he did not take any step at that time to make them as party to the case and then proceeded with the case. Even no prayer for amendment was made before the trial court during the trial of the case. In a case reported in 1984 B.L.D. (AD)-27 (Jalaluddin Fakir Vs. Shahjahan Ali Molla and others) their lordships hold the view, which was also held in 33 D.L.R. (AD) 113, which is as follows." 33 DLR? (AD) 113 has laid down the law regarding necessary parties in a pre-emption application under sec-tion 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. There is has been held-"The right of pre-emption as provided under sub-section (1) of section 96 is a statutory right.. The cause of action, for pre-emption of any transfer accrues to the Co-sharer tenants and contiguous land owners. The right of the applicant of applicants claiming to be co-sharer tenants of owner of contiguous land, is not absolute but subject to the right of other Co-sharers and other holders of land contiguous to the land transferred as the case may be for proper adjudication. To give full effect to the statutory provision, all the necessary parties must be impleaded because relief cannot be given in the absence of such party." 

 7. The learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted that before trial of the learned Assistant judge the opposite party No. 1 prayed for supply all the necessary parties to the case and the petitioner by a petition supplied necessary parties and he made all of them parties in this case, so the petitioner cannot say at this stage about defect of parties of the case and even if the case is of defect of parties it is mere omission and omission of such par-ties may be added at any stage of the case. I cannot accept this submission in view of the decision reported in 1984 D.L.R. (AD)-27 wherein their lordships held that the respondent did not disposed her name to impleaded her by ascertaining in the instant case after filing the kabala stated above. So knowing fully well of this defect he continued the case without impleading to a parties to the case. The learned sub-ordinate judge without considering all the fact and circumstances of the case send the case back on remand, as the appeal preferred before him which was not for only on preliminary points. In this view of the matter I am unable to agree with the findings and decision of the appellate court. In view of the above discussion I find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.
